utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor, counsel, the interpreters, the technical booth. Are we all set and ready? Yes, we are. We shall continue with the hearing with Professor Bianchini. Good morning, Professor Bianchini. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning. Dear colleague, good morning. Mr. Prosecutor, Professor Bianchini. So this morning we shall resume and pick up where we ended yesterday, and that is questions through the counsel, defence. I would kindly ask the usher to pass to Professor Bianchini the exhibit, exhibit numbers 116, 119, 126 in order to be able to compare them. 116, 119, and 126. Stefano Bianchini (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we discussed the issue that at the meeting in Villa Konak on the 7th and 8th of March, 1992, between Messrs. Boban, Izetbegovic, and Karadzic, the principles of the new order of Bosnia and Herzegovina were discussed, and here as exhibit 116 we have the map based on that. Do we have it? Yesterday, we also stated that the division on this map coincides practically to the Vance-Owen Plan which followed about a year later. If we take into consideration these two maps with set-up of the ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, bearing this in mind, I will kindly ask you, Professor, for your comments concerning the decision, the exhibit 126, on the establishment founding of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Here you can see that this was published in the national gazette in September 1992 and it is based on the session on the 3rd of July, 1992, when the decision was adopted in this form. Do you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly because the problem is that the document, as you can see, is of November 18, 1991. So it was published in the official gazette in September 1992; that is more or less one year later. I think for the simple reason that in November 1991, they didn't have any official gazette. The official gazette started to be published after July 1992. So this is, I think, the reason that they wanted to give a more official meaning to a decision, in fact, made one year earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I agree, Professor, but, please, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the initial decision from November 1991 was amended and supplemented at the session of the third of July, 1993. Therefore, the final form of the decision which was published in the official gazette and was published on the 7th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please, take into consideration the introduction of the decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm just thinking if the elements that were included instead of that -- it was only the so-called, in English it is "The reasons." So this part: While all the decision about the so-called basic, basic decisions, that is from the article 1 to the end are the same. So they added this part in this sense --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My question, Professor, sir, was: Do you agree that at the meeting on the 3rd of July, 1992, this decision, which was published in the national gazette, was given its final form and shape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As it has been stated in the introduction. Professor, could you comment on the point of this decision under 'I' on the reasons, heading "Reasons," which refers to the reasons for setting up the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. What is the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mention the first paragraph which means "Faced with ruthless aggression."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Army and Chetniks on the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia with the tremendous number of human victims with suffering and ordeals with the fact that the age old Croatian territories and goods are being taken away with the destruction of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its legally elected bodies, the Croatian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the difficult moments of its history, when the last Communist army of Europe united with the Chetniks is endangering the existence of the Croatian people and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is deeply aware that its future lies with the future of the entire Croatian people. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I wish to hear your comment on the reasons of why the community of Herceg-Bosna was set up on the basis of just what you have just read, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this document, it's clear that exist a common concern for the future of the Croatian people, both in Croatia and in the parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina where Croatian people still live. So the attention is particularly centred on the future of the Croat people and the ties between the two groups of Croats in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the focus of their concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. When you say that the focus is the survival of the Croatian people, can you comment in what framework? I would like to indicate to you parts of this decision where it speaks of the destruction of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also the endeavours for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, and where does the Croatian people see its place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's written about the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's written also with the destruction of the Republic which is considered as a matter of fact already in existence, and this is a document of July. Please, we have to take into account the two questions. When in April 1992 HVO was created, under article 2 of the document which was prepared and signed by Mate Boban, it is clearly stated that HVO has the duty to protect the territorial sovereignty of Herceg-Bosna and protect Croatian people. This is a very important point. And the second point is a document signed by -- I have this document -- signed by Mate Boban on the 10th of April, two days later, where it is written that the HVO represent the army of the Croatian people, because they don't accept the Territorial Defence, that is the Bosnian army, as their own military army because they don't have any confidence in it. So in this sense, I think that considering these two documents before, the attention is that they are already declaring that Bosnia-Herzegovina doesn't exist anymore, and they are particularly interested, albeit they repeat the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The focus of the interest of this document is that they are particularly concerned with the Croats fate in Croatia and in Herzegovina, but not in the general -- in the general context of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to focus on the commenting of this document which has been submitted as an exhibit here. Later on, we will pass on to other documents. Could you agree with the conclusion, sir, that in the text of this document, as the reason for setting up the community of Herceg-Bosna, that it will be set up due to the ruthless aggression of JNA and Chetniks in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the destruction of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, third that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina will support a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, and article 5 of this document on the second page, that the community, community of Herceg-Bosna, will respect and recognise the legally elected bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are these the basis for setting up the community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just add, to agree with you -- to this question, that one is written on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is added that but always emphasising that they are protecting their own historical area and the interests of the entire Croat people. There own historical area means that they were particularly interested in protecting Herzegovina, not the whole Bosnia, not Bosnia as a whole. So it's -- it's possible to understand from this document that there are some kind of cautious or preventions in participating or in saving the whole Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that it's a document from which we can understand that very early has been taken into account that Bosnia-Herzegovina has disappeared very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would ask you again, Professor, to answer the question which has been put. Do we, from this document, on the basis of the text which was also published in the official gazette, does it indicate that Herceg-Bosna was founded in view -- due to the reason of the JNA and Chetniks' aggression, its destruction for the creation of independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and for the independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, these are the postulates of this decision, and do you agree that the reasons for setting up a Bosnian community was in the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... contained the following sentence: On the emphasis, I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- your question that in all the topics, in all the topics you mentioned, you include that this sovereignty has been, in a way, considered that the Croatian Democratic Union emphasised that they are protecting their own historical area and the interests of the entire Croatian people. If you include this, I agree. If you don't include, I can't be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, Professor, sir, of course I include that particular thesis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, but your dialogue is quite interesting, but one should bear in mind the fact that you have interpreters mediating in your dialogue, and since you tend to reply immediately, the interpreters are unable to finish the translation and to translate your statements in full whereas everything which you say is extremely important, so please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence apologises for asking the questions too quickly. We should certainly bear that in mind henceforth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, Professor Bianchini, bearing in mind this particular provision that the primary task is to defend those parts of the sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina in which the ethnicity which we're talking about lives, of course bearing that in mind but with a view to the defence of part of the territory just as a part of the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you then agree that the reason for the establishment of Bosnia and Herzegovina is, as indicated, with the respect for the democratically legally elected authorities as proclaimed in article 5 of this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can agree if it's clear that there existed this kind of peculiar accent on the aspect of the protection of Croatian areas instead of whole Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The protection of the Croatian parts but within the framework of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Croats. It's not for the Muslims and the others leaving Bosnia. This is the crucial question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I agree. But going back again to an attempt to calm the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the part of the international community from the attempt in Villa Konak to the Vance-Owen Plan, and taking into consideration all these endeavours on the part of the international community to resolve the question in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I should like to ask you for your comment whether this decision, on the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, especially with reference to article II which states what municipalities shall form part of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, does this fit in or, rather, is this a logical sequence of the agreement, exhibit 116, from the Villa Konak and later of Vance Owen's plan. I should like to kindly ask you to take stock of the names of these municipalities and to compare the municipalities which comprise -- are comprised in the map which is exhibit 116 and map which is part of exhibit 126. So, please, does the indication, the designation of municipalities from the decision on the establishment of a Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, does it coincide with the division shown in this map which was made under the auspices of the international community? Professor, sir, perhaps it would be of help to you in answering this question to have the map from the Vance-Owen Plan which I have copied from the book of Karlo Rotim which is the defence of Herceg-Bosna where the municipalities are described by name, and this map which is in the file, the court file, you cannot see the names of municipalities, so I should like to ask the usher to come and pass this map to Professor Bianchini. Of course, I have copies also for my colleagues from the OTP and for Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is exhibit number D6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the decision of creating a Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna with adding this part, the Reasons of July, but the community of Herceg-Bosna was created in November 1991. That is -- sorry. The list of the -- in the article II, the list of the municipalities which are included here is the same. So in this case, it's correct to say that they were preparing -- they were -- this area, which is included in the Vance-Owen Plan, which is included in the Konak more or less, because the difference is little -- the differences are little, have not only the document in between of this document we are speaking about that is of July 1992 but we have also the previous decision of November 1991, in which the list of the municipalities is the same. So if you can consider that the international community in a way considered to establish an area with a majority of Croatian population which corresponded with the list of the municipalities claimed by the Croatian community since November 1991, this is correct. Since November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to ask you for a small comment also, going back to our conversation of yesterday, regarding the document that you mentioned from November 1991. Will we agree that -- it was a party document, and that it was a document about the Croatian Democratic Union as a political party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas what was published in the official gazette is a different form of document than a party document; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not so much. Not so much. Take into consideration the peculiar situation and the political culture of people of that time, so if you consider from the international point of view, from the legal international point of view --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- ex post, you can consider one is the party, one is a institutional organisation, which was not anyway agreed with the government of Bosnia. This is an autonomous decision. So this is -- this institutional framework is not coming from an agreement within the government and established in this sense, it's an autonomous decision. It is a claim, in a sense. Anyway, taking into consideration that the political culture and the mentality of the time was so that institutional building and the role of the party had not so clear and evident borders in between the two things, I think that we have to take into account this peculiar political aspect. We cannot remain close to a mere legal interpretation which I can understand from different point of view, but if you ask from my point of view, the answer can't be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're probably right, Professor Bianchini. That is a form of legal question rather than a question for an expert of your vocation. Let us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry. No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not a question of my -- only of my peculiar -- particular orientation. I would contest an only legal interpretation of these two documents because you can't have a legal interpretation only if you don't take into account also the peculiar political culture and mentality of the policymakers at that time when the documents were prepared. So it's not only a question of my peculiar -- this is one -- because I'm very sensitive in this sense because sometimes I have a lot of discussions with other experts in the international context when they move only from "legal external point of view." This doesn't work in the context of the former Yugoslavia. We have to take into consideration that these elements must be compared with the peculiar mentalities, situation and political culture within. Otherwise, the result is that of Vance-Owen. They thought -- they thought to have a mediation in order to create two, three, ten cantons, two, three areas with an ethnic majority in order to save the sovereignty of Bosnia. But the interpretation inside was they are legitimising us, so we have to continue this in order later to erase the sovereignty of Bosnia because this was the interpretation, this was the reason why Messrs. Vance Owen and Owen Stoltenberg shared the responsibility in this sense, because they didn't take into account the peculiar mentality of the people who were negotiating with them, and I think that this has to be taken into account. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, I can absolutely agree with you that it is very easy to interpret events exposed and it is quite another matter when we do it in this way. Let us leave, however, these documents aside for the time being. I will now pass onto a subject which has to do with the establishment of the sovereign Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the developments which ensued as well as touch upon the links between the sovereign republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia as former republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So let us proceed from the beginning. Will you please be so kind as to repeat for the benefit of the trial chamber when was the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the governmental point of view, it was immediately after the referendum, the outcomes of the referendum were known, so in March -- March 1992, albeit from the international point of view, the recognition was on April 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So April 6th. April 6th, 1992, the international community recognised the sovereignty of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall which state, from among the international community thereafter was the first or among the first to recognise the sovereignty of Bosnia -- of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and more specifically on the 7th of April, the second day after, in 1992, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The international reaction, it was the United States, Croatia, and other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So a day after, the international community had recognised the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina; Croatia has self-recognised the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you comment on this? How do you comment on this speedy recognition on the part of Croatia, because we know that many other countries did so much later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have in the exhibit the decision signed by the President Tudjman on this, and we have had the opportunity to comment already on this subject, so I don't have any other evidence to stress in the context of the former Yugoslavia. It was in a sense understandable the recognition from Croatia because it was expected that from the international community that the country recognised just a few months earlier did this step, particularly because otherwise the suspicion that Croatia might have territorial claims immediately on Bosnia would have endangered the recognition -- you see that in the recognition, it was stated that they recognised the state -- this was before the Badinter commission made known his -- its opinion, that is, between December 1991 and January 1992, it was stated that recognition was followed only grant that a state has no claims, territorial claims, towards neighbours. So it was in this sense expected. But the same document of the President Tudjman included the famous recognition, dual recognition of citizenship, which was not agreed with the government of Bosnia. This was unilaterally a decision included in the recognition, and this created immediately concern and difficulties between Zagreb and Sarajevo. Immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We shall come to that, Professor, sir. So on the 7th of April, Croatia recognised the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After that, there were contacts established at the level of the governments of the two states, and here I particularly have in mind the contact established between the presidents Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman in Zagreb on the 21st of July in 1992. I have here the text of the agreement. Unfortunately, for technical reasons, we have not managed to have it translated and will do so subsequently, but I do have a copy for you, for the registry, for the colleagues from the OTP, but I should like you to see this document so that we can hear your comments on it. I should like to ask the usher to pass the document to the professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, are you familiar with the text of this agreement. So it emanated from the meetings between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Tudjman on July 21, 1992, in Zagreb. Can you comment on this agreement for our benefit in brief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, because it's -- some of the copies are not -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Quite generally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document that was attempting to establish a kind of military alliance between Croatia and Bosnia which was not in effect -- this was the aim particularly of Mr. Tudjman. But a complete military alliance had been rejected by Izetbegovic at that time. So the compromise was this document. So this is in general. Then we can speak about some specific point, if you want. What is very important is that point 6 is that HVO is a part of the army of the Bosnian army; so is considered in this document as a part of the Bosnian army, which was not so clear before. The second question is that the two countries agreed to cooperate militarily alongside the borders, alongside the borders of the two countries, and they made a decision, and this is the point, point 8, that a military alliance will be taken into account effectively only if the international community will be unable to stop the aggression. So in this sense, in this sense, the document is, albeit some of my colleagues consider it a document as a military alliance, I think it is -- we need to have a more cautious evaluation of this document as a document of creating -- aimed at creating better relations between the two countries, taking into account that concerns and tensions were already growing between Croat authorities and Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this is your general interpretation. I should like to ask you for a couple of specific interpretations. I shall read the text to you so that the text can be translated and then I will ask for your comment. We are now on item 1. The president of the presidency of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the president of the Republic of Croatia have agreed that the future state set-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall proceed from the principle of full equality of the three titular peoples, the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs. The constitutional and the political order of the country shall be based on the constituent units in the establishment of which care shall be taken of the national, historical, cultural, economic, traffic, and other elements. I am kindly asking you for a comment of this item.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The comment is that Izetbegovic, with this point, accepted the idea that Bosnia-Herzegovina will be transformed into a state which is based on areas where the three titular nations have a dominant role in considering this area with an integration of cultural, political, economical -- which is included in the claim of -- when Herceg-Bosna was created in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you considered this document a military alliance, on the one hand, but is it just a military alliance? I am pointing to the text of the document which refers to the following issues: Item II namely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't consider this a military alliance, so I would -- my colleagues sometimes interpret this in this sense. I am more cautious, and I consider this a document attempting to make, create better conditions for improved relations between Croatia and Bosnia. So it is a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Item 2 refers to the fact that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia will cooperate. Now, line 3. As regards the questions of the economy, financial, and energy -- industrial and energy field cooperation, cooperation in restoring life in the demolished areas, the addressing of property questions, of physical and legal persons, the coordination of social services in the respective states, and in particular, in the field of work, of labour, social and welfare policy, health, education, science, culture, physical culture, scientific and technical cooperation, cultural and educational cooperation, information, and religious matters. So we see that we're talking here about a very comprehensive form of cooperation, complex cooperation, covering all fields of life of a community. Can I have your comment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a -- as you know is a general -- general agreement, a general framework, where then you have to go into details, but it's a general agreement on the basis of which the two leaders decided to cooperate in all these fields described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, item 3 of this document. The State delegation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina expresses its gratitude to the Republic of Croatia for having accepted or taken in and caring for refugees from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in exceeding its possibilities. I shall just like to remind you of a fact which was aired on the 9th of May at the press conference in 1992, 9th of May, and that was that on the 9th of May, 1992, practically at the time of this period, Croatia had already taken care for 228,000 refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina which was around 5 percent of the total population of the Republic of Croatia at the time. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot of -- a larger part of the population from Bosnia, when the war started, fled the country, and, of course, because of the borders, they went immediately to Croatia when they did not -- didn't go outside the former Yugoslavia at all. In this sense, Croatia received a wave of refugees, and this is an article where it is appreciated the contribution of the Croatian government in order to give hospitality to the refugees from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, are you perhaps aware what the national composition of this number of refugees was, these refugees who found shelter in the Republic of Croatia and came from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The large majority of them, I don't know the exact percentage, but the large majority were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Item 4 of this agreement: "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia will cooperate also in the field -- internal affairs and the judiciary." Item 5: "The President of the Republic of Bosnia and the President of the Republic of Croatia have agreed that in further pursuing their cooperation, they shall meet regularly, at least twice a year." Can you agree with the conclusion, Professor, that here we are talking about an endeavour of long-term cooperation through direct bilateral contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have to take into account the interpreters who do not have the document. As for item 6, you have already made comment in your introductory statement, which is that the Republic of Croatia, the HVO was a constituent part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Please comment on paragraph 2 of item 6, and I'll read it now for the sake of translation. "The temporary civilian authorities, the provisional civilian authorities, which were created in the war conditions within the framework of the Croatian Defence council, shall be coordinated and established -- shall be brought into compliance as soon as possible with the constitutional order of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on which talks shall be immediately initiated in the spirit of the principle referred to in item 1 of this agreement." Let us remind ourselves, item 1 is the agreement of the -- about the future constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina upon the principles of the full equality of the constituent peoples, the Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats. Can you comment upon this part of the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the one hand, this was a clear and evident rejection of some of the sentences included in the documents which created the HVO on the 8th of April, 1992, and which followed the 10th of April. So in this sense, it was clear that HVO was not another army because the Croatian people did not recognise as its own army, the Bosnian army, but here you see that the -- under the pressure, evidently under the pressure of the Croatian government, it recognised that HVO is a part of the army, so the Croatian people recognised as its own the army of Bosnia as its own army, taking part in the command. This was the decision. And secondly, second sentence is that an agreement has to be started, a negotiation has to be started in order to adopt the evolution of the situation as far as concerned the autonomy of Herceg-Bosna in the framework of a new Bosnian -- a Bosnian state. So this is the comment for the two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, please pay attention to the first word in the second paragraph. It says temporarily, provisional civilian authorities. Do you agree that this agreement at the level of the presidents of the two states has laid down that the forms of organisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina were of a temporary, provisional nature, as far as the civilian authorities were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I knew, this was temporary, because it was not included this term "temporary" in the previous Herzegovinan document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it was temporary. We agree on that. Do you agree that as regards further developments, it said that there were would be further negotiations, and it also referred to the fact that the two presidents would be meeting twice a year. The issue was not defined, namely, fully through the existing document but would have been negotiated and further shaped in future negotiations; do we agree that that was the gist of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was the aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, a while ago you referred to the context of the acquisition of citizenship, so would you please pay attention to item 7 which I shall now read for translation purposes. I am quoting item 7: "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia shall mutually make it possible for each other's citizens to acquire dual citizenship."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the recognition that a mutual -- mutual, double citizenship might be accepted according to this. This is mutual. This is very important, this term "Uzajamno." "Mutual." This means concerns not only Bosnia but also Croatia. As you know, as you know, the Croatian constitution was amended last December and Muslims were erased as a nationality or minority in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The same happened with the Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know. Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have already commented partially on item 8 in your introduction to the -- so I would like to focus on paragraph 2 of item 8, which has to do with the joint position of the two presidents to the effect that there was continued aggression of Serb and Montenegrin forces on the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, in this context paragraph 2 says, and I quote: "To that end, both States shall continue their hitherto successful cooperation and permanent coordination of their defensive operations in the border zones between the two States." Mr. Professor, can you agree when I say that even before this agreement, there was successful cooperation and that it was said that it would continue in the border zones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I don't agree. This is a sentence to show a situation of cooperation which, in fact, didn't exist. What happened -- there existed, some kind of cooperation, at the beginning when it was not clear for the population the first weeks of war. It was not clear what was going on. You know, the Serbs and Montenegrin -- the JNA attacked, and attacked particularly in eastern Bosnia, eastern Bosnia, and western Bosnia, in order to create a corridor between these two areas. So a lot of people, particularly Muslim and generally people who did not heavy weapons, they started to fight or because they wanted to defend the family, the house, just these things. And then they -- when they found the others -- other people fighting with them, they joined. So in the first weeks, you had Muslim people joining the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina and you had Croatian people joining the army of Bosnia in Central Bosnia. This was at the beginning. And later, this polarised. When it happened, this. One thing that was not known at the time, but you have in evidence in the exhibit -- sorry, in the evidence of the document of Bobetko, the 12th of April, Bobetko gave the first order to leave off the insignia of the Croatian army in Bosnia, and then before this agreement, when Mostar was freed by the army -- by the Croatian army and the HVO, the government in Bosnia expected to have help in order to stop the siege of Sarajevo, but the HVO didn't pay any effort to do this, and this created great concerns. For this reason, they went to Zagreb and they signed this kind of sentence in order to hope to stop these kind of tensions growing and to create the best condition for future cooperations. But speaking about past good cooperation, it seems to me that it was -- they were policymakers so they interpreted, but the situation on the ground was a little bit different, and the sentence was -- in the terms they hoped in the future to have this while claiming that it was already in the past, but it was not exactly the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Be that as it may, we do have before us an official document signed by the highest representatives of two sovereign states. I suppose that we cannot say that this particular sentence, which I ask you to comment on, is false, or can we say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's diplomatic sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of the same item, paragraph 3 of the same item says that unless there is an immediate end put to the aggression on the states that -- and that is the last sentence, and I'm quoting -- "all the necessary forms shall be considered -- all the necessary forms of broader cooperation shall be considered and implemented in the military field as well as a coordination of military operations for the purpose of the definitive repelling of the danger which was threatening the two states." Can we agree that this refers to aggression on the part of the Serb and Montenegrin armies on the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the registry to -- I should like to tender this as a defence exhibit and I should like the registry to take it into consideration as such and mark it with the next number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Do you have a comment, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We object to the tender of it only on this basis: Until we've been able to read it fully, when the translation is available. So I don't expect, at the end of the day, to be objecting to it, but I do object now because I can't read it and I don't know what it says other than what has been interpreted through Mr. Mikulicic. So once the translation is available and we've read it, I don't think there should be any difficulties, but at this stage we do object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Niemann is right, I believe. I feel that we cannot admit the document without a translation, so we can speak about the document as we have spoken about the constitution which also has not been tendered into the file, but I do not think that it is possible for it to be tendered as an exhibit without a translation. So once we do have the translation, you will be able to ask for it to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The defence has apologised because of the technical impossibility to also append a translation to this document, but it will certainly do so in the further course of the proceedings, and then we shall ask Your Honours for it to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked just for the purposes of identification as defence exhibit number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This agreement that we have been talking about, both the presidents -- the agreement states the wish of both presidents to continue meeting with a view to implementing the agreement which they reached. Can the usher please pass exhibit 126 F to the professor? So that is a document of the United Nations dated April 26, 1993. It is a letter whereby Mr. Mario Nobilo, the ambassador attached to the United Nations, the Ambassador of the Republic of Croatia, submits to the president of the Security Council and attached to this letter is a joint statement of Messrs. Izetbegovic and Mate Boban in connection with a meeting that was held in Zagreb on the 24th of April, and, please, I draw your attention to the date, that is two days after the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement -- no, I'm sorry. No, I apologise. You have commented on this joint statement. However, I am sorry, I apologise. I have the wrong sequence in my documents, so I withdraw this question and I shall start again. Will the court usher please pass this document to the professor? Of course, I have a copy for the Chamber and for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence exhibit D8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this is a document dated April 22, 1993. It is an appeal of the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman. Are you familiar with this document, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you just look at it briefly and give us a brief comment on what the purpose and the contents of the document are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know generally because I know Mr. Tudjman made this kind of appeal in order to stop the tension -- the clash, the military clashes, that already were spreading in Bosnia between Muslims and Croats. This is this declaration which was based on the one side on international pressures on Mr. Tudjman on the other side because an alliance with the Muslims, it's understandable, it might be in the interests of the Croatian government, considering official position made in other situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, you say that this is a document where President Tudjman is appealing for a cessation of the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina between the Croats and the Muslims, so that is April 22nd, 1992 -- 1993. And the last paragraph of this document, if you will be so kind, we shall read it: "For the sake of peace and preservation of strategically important Croat-Muslim alliance, as well as for the sake of implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, I welcome readiness expressed by the Croat and Muslim leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic, to meet with the co-chairman of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia, Lord David Owen, in Zagreb, 24 April 1993." I give you the exhibit we looked at before, and that is exhibit 126 F. So on the basis of an invitation in Zagreb on the 24th of April, under the auspices of Lord David Owen, there was a meeting attended by Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. The outcome of this meeting was a joint declaration, a joint statement, as stated in document 126 F. Can you give us a general comment on this meeting and the results of the meeting as embodied in the joint statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the statement, it's very important, I think, particularly point 2, with it's written that the signature is -- of this joint statement, "... hereby order all military units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Croatian Defence council to immediately cease fire and all hostilities in all areas where such military units are in contact." This is a clear evident effort to stop military clashes with the hope that they can remain incidents and not a war. So this was the reason. About the result, as you know, the document didn't have any serious consequence because the war continued and even the tensions worsened rapidly in May and June. So in this sense. But this was an attempt to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Item 4 of this joint statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Mikulicic, for interrupting, but we have some technical problems with the video monitor. I think anyway it is a convenient point to take a break, a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: --- Reconvened at 10.45 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, we ended with this last document of the 25th of April, 1993, which represents and has been sent through the permanent representative of Croatia, and it is a document of the joint statement on the meeting held in Zagreb in April 1993. You, in your introduction, gave an explanation and a global commentary of this document. I would like to ask now for some additional comments, if I may? So we do agree, I assume, and if not -- so this is really a document which is a consequence of the attempts to stop the conflict between the units of the Croatian and Bosnian people in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So let us focus on item 4, and I would kindly ask you to give us a more detailed commentary of it, and what does this item really represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statement is very clear in this sense, it confirms that the military clashes between the army of Bosnia and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Units of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Units of, military clashes between units anyway -- units of HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina, are contrary to the policy of the representatives of the two peoples and the continuation of such conflict would seriously jeopardise the achievement of their political goals, that is, the independence and territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the framework of the Vance-Owen Plan accepted and signed by the signatories of this statement and success in the fight against the aggressors who wants to break the state apart, occupy the territories and annex the occupied territories to greater Serbia. The sentence I think is very clear and evident in its meaning and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we may agree that the meaning of this item is, that is, that the conflict between the units of the Bosnia army and the HVO go against the common policy, namely, the achievement of independence and territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the framework of the Vance-Owen Plan which was signed previously. That is the meaning; do you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the exact meaning of the said diplomatic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I remember that when you, in your introductory commentary, you indicated the peculiarity, namely, this witness for this document, as a witness we have the signature of Dr. Tudjman. In view of the preceding document, the appeal of President Tudjman which we have just seen, which was issued two days earlier in which he calls in line with the Vance-Owen Plan, the leaders, Bosnian Croatian leaders in a meeting in Zagreb under the auspices of Lord Owen, isn't it then in this context, isn't it also quite normal that, as a host, it is Dr. Tudjman who will be signing -- who appealed for this meeting and who also launched the initiative for this meeting? Could we -- could you agree with this explanation of the signature of President Tudjman on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only to a certain extent in the sense that if you consider that the initiative started from Tudjman, in that context, yes, no problem. But, this event was in a particular context, that is the context of the dismemberment of Yugoslavia, in which the difficulties in relations within Croatia and Bosnia, the need -- the need that Tudjman had in a way to have formal good relations with Izetbegovic, I would like to emphasise that when in July 1992, Izetbegovic and Tudjman met and signed the agreement you attended before, the first aim of Tudjman was to have a military alliance in order to legitimise the Croatian army presence in Herzegovina which was not, in the end, the result of the meeting. So in this sense, he was urged because he needed this to do. We know from the legal point of view it is one thing, but we have to take into account again the ground -- we are speaking about policymakers, and they use different tools in order to achieve their own goals. So in this sense, I understand from the formal point of view he invited <name unclear>, but behind this we have to take into account he wanted this because he was the protector of Mate Boban. This is the crucial question. So he was the person in this sense involved in the question, and he knew very well that he had the army, the question of saving the alliance with in a sense the Muslims was because even Croats will be threatened by the offensive of the JNA in a sense, so he had different arguments to do this, but we have to take it into account in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course. But we must also take into account that the meeting was held under the auspices of the international community, namely, personified in Lord Owen; do you agree? Could you comment on page 4 of this document which represents an agreement of the representatives of the Bosnian and Croatian peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina and military representatives, General Halivovic and General Petkovic respectively. I would like to ask you for a short commentary on this annex. Item 1: "BiH army and the HVO will retain their separate identities and command structures. Their functions will include all aspects of personnel, logistic, administration, training, morale, and identity. They will form a joint command which will be responsible for the operational control of military districts. The joint command will consist of two commanders in chief, General Halilovic and General Petkovic will meet on a regular basis, at least weekly." Could you comment this obviously military agreement is a consequence and follows the political agreement signed on the same day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if the term "military agreement" is exact because I don't know what we can mean by this term exactly. If you think that military agreement is military agreement between two army -- as, for instance, the Croatian army and the Bosnian army, this is not the case. This is a case of an agreement of two -- between two units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the state, so we have to take into consideration that we are speaking about the framework of one state. And this is a very interesting document because this is the attempt, maybe the last -- and, in fact, I think this was the last attempt -- to find a compromise. I think this is the better word, a "compromise," in order to establish a mutual recognition of two military units. In a sense, this is from Izetbegovic’s point of view a step back on the position he wanted to support during the meeting in July 1991 when it was stated the HVO is a part of the Bosnian army. Here is already -- is already envisaging some kind of confederation. Two different armies with a joint command which can meet every week -- weekly. So in this sense, it's a compromise. It was a compromise that didn't work at all, as we know, but this was the attempt at stopping the clashes in order to create some kind of military confederation of two units within the same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We'll leave this document and I'd kindly ask the usher to present to the witness another document which the defence will introduce and tender as an exhibit and we would like to hear his comment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, sir, are you acquainted with this statement which followed the meeting of Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban in Mostar on the 2nd of April, 1993, and which also speaks of the document which was just analysed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is also before the military clash occurred in Travnik, five days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a general comment on this meeting on the basis of this joint statement of the two representatives of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I would only ask you to take into account the date, this is the 2nd of April, and also to take into account the date when the Muslims signed the Vance-Owen Plan, that was the end of March 1993. So it was signed eight days after the signature of the Vance-Owen Plan by the Bosnian side and Mate Boban signed it in January of that year. Would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is another statement in this context you mentioned. Another statement in order to stop clashes which occurred between the units of HVO and Bosnian Herzegovinan army as stressed in point 5 as well as in point 1. The document is taking into consideration particularly what happened in -- because this was in April, so before the clashes in Travnik but after what happened between January and February in Busovaca. So in this context, when the -- Izetbegovic, as their side accepted to sign the Vance-Owen Plan, which is important to take into consideration, the Vance-Owen Plan was based on different documents, and these different documents were submitted and prepared not only in January but even in February and March. So this was, because the government of Izetbegovic wanted to have some more guarantees and discussion continued. And then we have -- so in this context, this statement is again an attempt of stopping clashes, military clashes, which already occurred since -- as we have information since the middle of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So generally we may agree that this was another one of the attempts of the two sides, a mutual attempt of the two sides involved in the conflict to resolve those tensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't solve the conflict. They attempted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: An attempt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a formal attempt to give information to the army not to clash each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, now, remembering the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement from July 1992 which was jointly agreed that the two Presidents would be meeting and contacting on the basis of that agreement, did such meetings follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, yes. I'm not so sure that it was exactly two times per year all the time, but they had often meetings together. As well as, you know, Tudjman and Milosevic had, Tudjman and Milosevic met 48 times during the war period, so this was in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Professor, anything about the meeting between the two Presidents in September of that year in Geneva? I would kindly ask the usher to give the Professor -- to pass the Professor that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence exhibit D10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the two Presidents met in September of that year in Geneva on the basis of the earlier agreements that they would be contacting and meeting in order to find solutions to the problems? Is this joint declaration another attempt to resolve the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina; would you say that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a certain extent. I read the document, and I was immediately interested by a specific point which I found new -- the origin of new concerns and contrasts between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina which is very interesting. Let me find the point. It's the point on -- because the pages were ... When they speak about a union -- where is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, first I should like to try to confirm certain points. Could we consider this document as an attempt of the two Presidents to resolve the conflict which happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely, they agreed on the setting up of working groups, and these groups would have to consider and deliberate the problems connected with the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here I am primarily thinking of paragraph 1, items 4, 5, and 6 of it. Then item 3 where we see the names of these -- the people heading working groups which were to resolve these questions. In this sense, it is a new attempt to resolve the situation which has been created in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, only to a certain extent. It's true that I can also -- here they made the decision to provide, as you can see at point 2, here on the second page, "Provide for bilateral and unconditional disbanding of all detainee camps," for instance, which didn't occur. But this was -- they had a lot of meetings, they agreed -- papers, papers, nothing on the ground. You can see particularly point 5: "Form a working group for matters related to the territorial delimitation between the two represent Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina including access to the sea." How long they discussed this question of access to the sea. It was immediately a question of concern and fighting until today, until today, because the question of Ploca, the question is under discussion till today between Tudjman and Izetbegovic. So I wanted to say that this is a document -- just one of the other papers signed without any effect, without any effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that this is one of the attempts, and you have said yourself there was a series of such attempts, to resolve this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we want to use a diplomatic terminology, yes, diplomatically, we can say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, sir, for the period we're talking about, from the date of recognition of the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then 1992, 1993, you have mentioned the term "diplomatic." What were the diplomatic relations between the two countries? Were they on the level of embassies with an exchange of ambassadors? Did they have diplomatic contacts? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they had diplomatic representatives. There was a diplomatic representative in Zagreb of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they tried to establish some contacts between them. I don't know when the representatives were established in the two capitals. And the ambassador came later because of the peculiar situation. It was, for many reasons, impossible for long time to enter Sarajevo, so this was one of the situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Croatian ambassador came to Sarajevo in June 1994, but can you remember when did the Bosnian ambassador come to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can presume immediately after the recognition. In Zagreb, there were -- Zagreb was not threatened by the war, so it was easier to establish --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, less than in Sarajevo, at least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, are you aware that in any time throughout 1992, 1993, and 1994, that the bilateral contacts between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were severed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. They were maintained for what was possible, contacts between the two states. And it was understandable why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have here another document which has the same fate as the document for which colleague Niemann lodged a complaint. It's a document in Croatian. I would just now submit it for filing. I will also later on submit the translation. The Professor understands the language. And if your Honour allows it, I would like to ask the Professor for a short comment of it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is identified as D11, only marked as such for the sake of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, what generally can you explain to the Trial Chamber what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an information sent by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Croatian Republic in which it informs them about the fact that they appointed a certain number of persons, six on one side and 21 on another side, as -- as a representative, economic and military representatives in Zagreb, and as a representative of the command of the Republic of Bosnia in Zagreb. So far as I understand, this is the information of people working in the embassy, in Bosnian embassy on these two topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you agree, Professor, that along the lines of this document, the conclusion derives, and this is a document from July 1993, and we can see that on the receipt seal of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, so can you agree that this document actually indicates that period, which is to say, July 1993 where, in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we had conflicts going on between the Croatian and Muslim units, so at that particular period the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had, in its military and economic representation branch, recruited quite numerous staff as well as in the logistical department of the main staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as in Split, but it can also be concluded on the basis of this document, this meant putting into practice ties between the two states also in the military field on the level of embassies. Do you agree to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I understand -- I know for the organisation of diplomatic activities, it seems to me that the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina in this sense was in a peculiar period at least -- action in Zagreb, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, we referred to, during today's conversation, that during the unfortunate events in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, despite the situation that it itself was, received a large number of refugees, that even Mr. Izetbegovic, along the lines of meetings between Tudjman and Izetbegovic, expressed their gratitude to the Republic of Croatia. I would ask the usher to pass to the professor, just for the sake of illustration of the subject that we are going to be discussing, exhibit number 120. That is the atlas map which you have constructed so that the trial chamber could follow more easily the situation being described on the terrain. So this is a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which you said was made according to your instructions. And I can make use of it at this particular moment only to ask you to explain to the Chamber what states does Bosnia and Herzegovina have borders on this specific map on the south-east and on the north-west?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina has borders with Croatia, from this line on this -- with this area (indicating) with Serbia and Montenegro formally. At the time of the war, Bosnia had as its borders the province -- so proclaimed independent Serb area of Krajina which was in this area (indicating) more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm then the conclusion that actually Bosnia and Herzegovina had a border on the one side with the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro whom it had proclaimed aggressors on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, on the other side, with its allies, their allies, in the self-styled Republic of Serbia Krajina, and on the third side a part of its border with the Republic of Croatia, the only part of the border which was passable at the time. Can you agree with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, in this time of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we, all of us, witnessed, as well as you yourself, the substantial humanitarian relief and aid which was granted by the international community to help the suffering people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what routes were taken by the humanitarian aid. How did it reach Bosnia and Herzegovina? I'm not speaking about the exact geographical location of the routes, but generally speaking ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can see from the map, it's evident that they had no other possibility to join Bosnia than across Croatia, Croatian territory. This is obvious, and particularly they had -- I can -- because I knew many of them who, particularly from Italy, gave great support to the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that -- was in Split, generally, and from Split they joined the other parts of Bosnia. Generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you agree, Professor, that despite the fact that in 1991 the United Nations imposed an arms embargo, that anyway a certain quantity of arms, let us say, found some concealed ways to reach the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the question of the transportation of arms, does the same apply as what we said for humanitarian aid, namely that arms reached Bosnia and Herzegovina via Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you agree, Professor, with the thesis that the Republic of Croatia could absolutely have cut off every delivery of both humanitarian aid and of weapons to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina had it wanted to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that thus the humanitarian assistance and the arms that came to Bosnia and Herzegovina came there with the knowledge and assistance of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a large extent, yes. To a large extent because I'm not so sure, for instance, for the army -- for the weapons coming from the Arabs or Islamic countries, but in other situations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, you just mentioned the question of Arabic, i.e., Islamic interests. Can you tell this Chamber what their role was, the role of that part of the world, apart from the European Community, the United States, and Russia, what was the role of the Arabic and Islamic countries in the conflict which was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already spoke about this topic before in past sessions. The Islamic community was deeply divided. They spoke a lot. They did less. They spoke a lot, particularly at international meetings, because they wanted to support the persistence of Islamic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was the aim. The other -- the problem is -- was that -- because the Islamic community was divided within, particularly Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Iran had different ideas of the evolution of (unintelligible). So the possible support coming from one -- part of the other countries might have different impact in this context. This is one thing. The second thing that they were aware that any move of the Islamic community in supporting strongly and effectively the Muslims in Bosnia would be -- would create concern in the international community and strengthen the -- one of the typical arguments of the Serb side that it was in Bosnia a war against -- of Christianity against Islamic world. This was also the same argument that was used by HVO when the clashes with the Muslims started. This is exactly the same. In the document, for instance, of April 1993, when the group of the HVO in Travnik sent the document to Messrs. Tudjman and Boban explaining what was -- in Travnik, they accused -- they charged Mujehadin to do this -- they used this term. It's true that Iran sent some groups of Mujehadin and we know that immediately after the date the agreement was signed. The United States made very strong control and forced these kind of people to leave the country, but they were a group of persons, and the impact -- the impact of this on the Islamic world -- on the Islamic world in Bosnia, which was, generally speaking, atheistic, in fact, to be Islamic was more because they wanted to distinguish themselves as ethnic community from the Croats and the Serbs than related to religious ideas, so the impact was only partial and had the opportunity to act, particularly with one stream of SDA, I mentioned several times yesterday this stream, which was in favour of the idea to accept even a partition of Bosnia and create a Muslimania. This was the goal of the fundamentalists, a Muslim state in order to create a core of Muslim spreading -- the Muslim religion into Europe as the first Muslim state of Europe. This was the famous -- but in January, if we speak about the Islamic community, even Turkey -- Turkey spoke a lot, but really, they did very -- so that -- it was so true that Izetbegovic was several times disappointed in the support, restricted support coming from the Islamic countries in comparison with its -- his expectations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Professor, that the Islamic world, they did not have a unified stand. You also said that -- say that also within the framework of the Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were different positions. What was the racial forces within the body of the Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina in view of these different attitudes, which forces were prevalent and which ones were in the minority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very difficult to say considering the condition of war. Very difficult to say, to have a clear picture. Take into consideration the evolution of events, I can conclude that this stream was a minority stream. How minor it was, this is difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which stream?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fundamentalists. It was made pressure, sometimes influenced Izetbegovic, but the other stream was a majority, take into account that they had the support of other -- other parts of the population which was not Muslim in the sense that supported SDA but they were, for instance, supporting other political parties' organisations, I mean the organisation of Zulfikarpasic, the SDP -- the Social Democrats Party -- former Communist left wing, or democrats who wanted to preserve the integrity of Bosnia and the integrity of Bosnia as a multi-cultural, multi-ethnic community. This part of the population was against the Vance-Owen Plan, the Owen Stoltenberg plan, and the Konak agreement. And they influenced the other stream of the SDA. So I think that in conclusion, the fundamentalist were a minority even in the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So generally observing -- observed and locally observed, can you agree with the thesis that in certain areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, these fundamental streams prevailed over these others, shall we call them, moderate streams among the Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, are you aware of the fact that foreign nationals, I mostly have in mind nationals of Islamic countries, joined during the events that we are discussing, those which took place in 1992, 1993, and 1994, joined the ranks of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and even, in fact, formed some of their own units, military units. Let me just remind you of a unit called Al Mujaheed which was in the third corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know this kind of brigade existed, and particularly the United States, no-- that this was one of the reasons of particular concern of the United States, and I don't disagree with you that this was one of the reasons why United States took the initiative in the beginning of 1994 to intervene in Bosnia and impose the federation -- the federation between the Muslim and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the United Nations. Will you tell us -- can you familiarise us with how, if -- what kind of a reaction, if any, did the European Community, i.e. the United Nations have to this phenomenon, particularly the reaction of the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes they expressed concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that this concern of theirs was expressed through official documents; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know this. Anyway, I know that concerns existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When we mentioned this Al Mujaheed which was part of the third corps, can you tell us in what area of Bosnia-Herzegovina were they located, if you know; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know. It seems just one, just one, was around Zenica, but I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we have agreed, Professor, on the fact that the Republic of Croatia had taken in a great number of Muslim refugees who had fled the war in Bosnia and came to the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and also that the Republic of Croatia made it possible for humanitarian relief and arms transported to pass through its territory to Bosnia-Herzegovina and also according to the agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic in the border areas between Bosnia and Croatia, there were units of the Croatian army. Please comment on this fact, in the light of the fact that we have such phenomena in today's world, and I am particularly referring to the role of Turkey in respect of the Kurdish population in its border areas and the role of Israel with respect to the Palestinians living in the border areas with Lebanon. Can you comment on this? Can you correlate these examples in a way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the Croatian position is concerned, you know, Croatia didn't have any other alternative than allow these volunteer humanitarian aid and even to allow the cross border transportation of illegal weapons. They could not stop because if they did this, the reactions of the -- the reaction of the international community would have been great, so strong that -- take into consideration that Croatia didn't control one-third of its territory -- with sanctions against Croatia in that situation, would push Croatia into a corner and Serbia would even have much more possibility to threaten Croatia and Bosnia than it might have had at the time. So this was a peculiar situation that must be taken into account. Croatia tried to obtain at that time, if possible, the support of the European Union or the United States while, I would like to stress, that in 1993, the international community was particularly surprised, particularly after June 1993, about the aggressive diplomatic position of Croatia towards Bosnia. This was evident -- so this was just to explain the different situation. As far as concern, the comparison with the Kurds or with the Palestinians, you know, national question is an open issue not only for the Balkans or for Yugoslavia and Bosnia, but is a question for international relations too. There are many countries that don't want to recognise ethnic groups -- this is the case of the Kurds, for instance -- because this means that they can claim to be a nation, and if they claim to be a nation, they can claim the state. This means a threat to the integrity of the state. So this is the reason why. This is one of the reasons why the international community was so weak in reaction -- in the reaction to the Yugoslav dismantlement, because they didn't have the instrument, the knowledge, and the ability to interfere. Even if they in different way understood, national principle is the principle which legitimise the state. So when you use the term "nation" in the United States it has a certain meaning, in Croatia another one. But when you speak about national rights, national rights of self-determination, immediately you create a situation which the European Community -- the international community and, generally, and generally the -- yes, the international community and the policymakers particularly, they have no other particular tools, instruments to interfere clearly making distinctions. So if you compare the Kurds, I can say that from this point of view, Turkey is working with the Kurds as well as the Serbs are working more or less with the Albanians in Kosovo. If you want to speak, you can make a similar -- similar position in the confrontation of Israel towards the Palestinians because of the concerns of the stability of the countries and so on. All these questions are unsolved because -- this is my peculiar position, of course, and this is one of the reasons of my disputes with some of my colleagues because the Yugoslav example made clear that we are at the end of the story for the national state and for the sovereignty of national states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, perhaps I didn't phrase my question rightly, so you did not answer my question the way I wanted. That is the question of the military intervention along the border areas of another state in the kind of case that we can see today in the relation between Turkey and Iraq and Israel and Lebanon. That was the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This creates concerns and these actions are condemned by international relations. Then you can argue why the international community condemned differently or used different tools in condemning these countries. This is another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with the fact that today in the modern world we are also faced with such situations whereby, in order to protect its own territory, a state intervenes in the border areas of the other state so as to prevent a threat to its own territory. For example, Israel treating the terrorist acts on behalf of PLO or the specific case of Turkey to protect itself against the terrorist acts of the Kurds. I do not mean to underestimate at all the sense of these actions, but just saying that these are acts which are in contravention of international law.
