utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even the reaction of the state is not allowed by international rules, you know, so both of the things are, in this sense, very disputed, and in the case of Bosnia, we have to take into account that there were not terrorist acts of the Muslims in Croatia that can justify this intervention. Take into consideration -- you are speaking -- more time you mentioned the Croatian army along the borders. They were not only on the borders, they were even in the centre. I don't think that Mostar can be considered on the borders. So I think that borders -- we can -- and probably from the legal point of view you can discuss for a long time what is the border and where is the border. But any way, taking into consideration the particular situation, I don't think that Mostar can be considered a border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What I had in mind in making this comparison were attacks by Serbs and Montenegrin -- and Serb and the Montenegrin army on the territory of Croatia from these southern parts, parts of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. But in this case, Croatian government had to receive a kind of invitation of a request from the Bosnian government to intervene in each state to support Tudjman and Izetbegovic--

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is the agreement Tudjman and Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can see in Herzegovina since the 12th of April. The agreement was in July. And in July, this agreement didn't allow to go through the borders. Just -- it was the cooperation on the borders, but not to have the army within the Bosnian state. So I think that in this -- this was the wish of Tudjman for this document, but this document didn't allow this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But it is explicitly stated in the agreement that in the case of a continued Serb and Montenegrin aggression, they would agree on further and wider military cooperation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If -- as I stated -- if the international community failed in these actions. In other words, you need again a claim, a request by Izetbegovic to enter the state, because otherwise, they can -- you can think that the Vance-Owen Plan, the Vance-Owen Stoltenberg plan, were other attempts of international community to stop the war. So this was not -- who judges in this case when is the moment to interfere? I think that in this case, the request to come into the territory -- in the territory of one state must be coming from the legal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It was along those lines that many negotiations were conducted that we have already made reference to before. Some were more successful, some were less successful, but generally, irrespective of the participation of the international community, there was generally little success; can you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally speaking I can say that all these agreements didn't have any outcome, positive outcome, until the intervention of the United States. On the other side, I would like to repeat that, albeit, we saw a lot of agreements, no one was clearly defining a military alliance between Bosnia and Croatia, and no one allowed the participation of Croatian army on the territory except for cooperation along the borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was talking about. I should now like to ask the usher to bring to the professor document 126 E. So this is a document of the Council of Europe declaration on the former Yugoslavia. Please pay attention -- I draw your attention to -- I believe it is not the whole document, however. I draw your attention to the time of the production of this document. Will you tell us at this time, the 11th and 12th of December, 1992, who was attacking the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina? That was actually the basis for the creation of this document, the adoption of this document. Who was attacking them in the areas of Sarajevo and other areas which are referred to in the document? Who is considered the attacking party in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the general point of view or in relation particularly to the Muslim-Croat relations? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Bosnian? From the general Bosnian point of view, as you can see in point 2 is written: "The primary responsibility for the conflict and its brutality lies with the present leadership of Serbia and of the Bosnian Serbs." It is presently correct -- very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will the usher please give the professor document 126 I? This is a document which is a statement signed by the President of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, and the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, signed in Geneva on the 17th of July, 1993, and this prompts me to ask the question, and that is the question which you have touched upon a number of times in your previous statement, and that is the question of the meeting in Karajorjevo and the outcomes of those meetings. First of all let me ask you: Have you had occasion in your research work so far to come across a document which had been published in connection with such -- with that meeting, with possible conclusions from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said during the previous sessions that we don't have any minutes of the meeting in Karajorjovo. We have only the public declaration of one of the members of the commission that was appointed by Tudjman and took part in the discussion with the Serb commission in order to prepare the maps immediately after Karajorjovo, and these meetings occurred during June, July, August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So tell us, Professor, do you know, roughly speaking, in the period from 1991 to the beginning of 1992 how many different meetings, plans, attempts at addressing the question of Bosnia and Herzegovina had there been within Bosnia-Herzegovina and outside Bosnia-Herzegovina under the auspices of the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many. I don't know the number, but many. As we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you at least approximately say what that number is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I can -- we can speak about the -- it depends when you want to start because we can include even the project of confederation, of Yugoslav confederation submitted by the European Union at the end of 1991, we can include the Cutiliero attempt at a negotiation, the Konak, which is connected, the plan of Lord Carrington, the Vance-Owen Plan, the plan of Owen-Stoltenberg, the Washington agreement, the Dayton agreement, and then you have maps and discussion with other persons because this is Karajorjovo, but also the meeting in Graz May 6 between Karadzic and Boban then they meet June 20 in Njivice, between representatives also of SDS and HDZ in order to find solution, and then, if I can remember, in a book published by Zdranko Tomac, in Croatia the title is "Qui a Tue la Bosnie?" -- "Who killed Bosnia?" is reported one part of one of these meetings -- if I can maybe check on my notes, I can be more sure, in this sense because it was written, it was written -- I don't remember if it was a meeting in between -- between Milosevic-Tudjman or between Mate Boban and Karadzic, so the level, I don't know, but it was established -- it was general agreement between the Serb side and the Croat side about the borders. It was in the book of Zdranko Tomac -- sorry, Zdranko Tomac was the Vice-President of Croatia in the government, coalition government in August 1991, and he was the leader of the SDP party, it was the party coming from the former League of Communists. And in this book of memoirs, he stated that the agreement -- quoted, he quoted one part of this public agreement, and the borders, the only two questions were the Serb side and the Croatian side were unable to find an agreement was, according to this document, the borders along the river Neretva. The Croatian side claimed all the city of Mostar, which is on one side -- on the other side of Neretva river, and the borders of the famous Banovina of 1939 which included one part of the left bank of the Neretva river, while the Serb side wanted only to have the borders alongside the river. So this was written in the -- but this was -- this is what has been published and what we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we may agree that there were many, many attempts at resolving the issue of Bosnia and Herzegovina through various meetings -- multilateral, bilateral -- plans, agreements, joint declarations, joint statements and so on and so forth. What does that actually mean? Can we in principle agree that this means that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was not at all easy to resolve in the very least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This means that -- this is my firm belief -- that it's impossible to find a negotiation amongst nationalisms, different nationalisms. The difficulty to find a solution in Bosnia was because the negotiations was made all by those who shared a nationalist approach, or by the European Unions, or the international community who tried to negotiate with them the other side -- the other part of the Bosnian question, that is the role of the civilian populations, the role of the oppositions, of anti-democratic -- sorry, anti-nationalist parties. I can just mention, for instance, for the Croatian side, the role that might be played by Komsic, the leader of the Croatian Peasant Party in Bosnia, and other people, such as these people, for instance, was very crucial, because something new happened after the agreement, the Washington agreement, and during the Dayton agreement, these people was, in a way, included in the three -- in the three delegations, the Serb the Croat, the Bosnian. So they were taking part in something new, but of course before the Dayton agreement, this was very interesting, a meeting was organised -- this was September 1995. I was there invited in Perugia, in Italy, and the representation of anti-nationalist organisations in Bosnia were all participating. There were Mr. Komsic from Croatian side, there was Mr. Dodik, the current Premier of the Republic of Srpska, Serb side, and there was Tocic from Tuzla -- I can't say Muslim side because he doesn't agree surely about this definition. So it was coming from the democratic areas of Tuzla, as you know, Tuzla, they saved all along the world the multi-cultural, multi-ethnic characteristic of the city. So this part was neglected and this was the reason why it was so difficult to find a solution, because the attention was all the time concentrated on nationalism. One has to take into consideration that the war in Bosnia was not, as we could see, claimed in all the documents, only a war between two or three sides: The Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims, but it was also a war against civilian populations. I think that it was primarily this, because in order to achieve the goals to have at least three areas with a predominant ethnic group or even the partition of Bosnia, it was very important to compel the population to accept this or moving the population or displacing -- sending them abroad, or killing the population, ethnic cleansing. This was a strategy that was included in the war. So those who supported this, even the fundamentalist, Muslim fundamentalist, we can mention again the <unintelligible>, were all responsible for this case, but the ideological responsibility is -- from my point of view has to be charged to nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the international community have a common approach to the resolution of the question of Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout this period? We've seen documents --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I wanted to remind the Villa Konak document and others, but the answer is "No." Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, we will take a break. The break will last 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: --- Resumed at 12.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, Professor, we may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to remove the document from the ELMO and to pass the document, the following document, 126 J. Once again, distinguished colleague, Mr. Niemann, I thank you for submitting this document to the file and we, as Defence, will be availing ourselves of it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to turn to the second page, Professor Bianchini, of the document. So it is a UN document we're referring to with which the Charge d'affaires of Croatia, Vladimir Drobnjak, the 9th November, 1993. From the document you can see that it follows the document of the 3rd of November, 1993, in which a request was made for an urgent meeting of the Security Council in connection with the events described in paragraph 2 of this document. So we are discussing here the Vitez area for which it said that it is the largest Bosnian Croat enclave in Central Bosnia. And to give the Trial Chamber a view of where this is, I will kindly ask the usher to give us exhibit 39 in order to be able to have a view of the area under discussion. Professor, please place the map on the ELMO, and show us the area discussed in the UN document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can take into consideration the largest one, this area (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the area, the area on the map, coloured with the prevalent Croatian population below 50 percent, which is mainly surrounded with a Muslim population, somewhere below 50 percent, or Gornji Vakuf and Zenica, the predominant population is over 50 percent. Do you agree with the content of the map? Now let us turn back to the UN document. In paragraph 2, it discusses the area of Vitez, the largest Bosnian Croat enclave in Central Bosnia, is seriously threatened by the Bosnian Muslim armed forces. Many reports have been received of military activity, that there are many, also, refugees. So we are dealing here with a conflict. Could you tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is described a military defeat of the Croatian army in Central Bosnia, and as a consequence of this, the battles, the fights in this area, started in September 1992, but they had a particular wave of clashes in the period between -- during all the summer. So at the end of the summer, the Croatian army was -- the HVO was defeated and the Muslim army was running into the villages. There were displaced people, as is described in this. Exactly -- this is a curious date when -- the 9th of November, 1993, the letter was sent. The same day the bridge in Mostar was destroyed by the HVO in Mostar. It was in one contest -- one situation; in another one, another one. In the context of the Central Bosnia, we are facing a situation in which the Muslim army was on the offensive and was moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And faced with the situation of numerous refugees and a population that has been encircled, I would like to introduce also an exhibit which should be passed on to Professor Bianchini.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence exhibit D12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bianchini, we have a motion for a resolution for the European parliament in Brussels of the 7th of November, 1993, a day later than the document we have just been discussing, the UN Security Council document. This is a document submitted by the Liberal Democratic Party and which has requested the European parliament and submitted a motion for a resolution. I would kindly ask you for comments for items A and C.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, the date is 10th of November. You told 7th. This is 10th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry -- it was -- this is a motion presented -- submitted by which party?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Liberal Democratic Reformists within the European parliament --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Parliament. Here you see there is emphasis on the situation where Bosnian Croats were found during that period trapped in Central Bosnia with -- in very great difficulties, and here is "fearing for the lives of the thousands of men, women, and children who have fled into the forest from their homes in Vares following the conquest of the town by Bosnian Muslim forces and who are the latest victims of ethnic cleansing." These are the points you mentioned. May I just -- interesting question. This is true, it was a great defeat and it was a great move of Croatian population at that time considering that the large percentage of Croats living in Bosnia were from Central Bosnia, not from Herzegovina. This question of Vitez -- of Vares is particularly interesting, is pointed in the document you see, the forests from their homes in Vares. What happened before Vares -- this was the end of go in, go out from the Muslim side and the Croatian side. In Vares, the mayor was a Croat mayor. And in Vares, this mayor sought to save multi-ethnic and multi-cultural relations with the Muslims in the months before this happened. He had the support of the Muslims, even when a great number of displaced people, Croatian displaced people, coming from other areas of Bosnia, went to Vares. And he opposed any pressures from the HVO to break relations with the Muslims. So HVO entered in Vares and compelled -- overthrew the mayor, threatened the mayor, and compelled the Muslim population to flee the village. Then, in reaction, the army, the Bosnian army intervened. There was another battle, battlefield, and then the HVO was defeated. This is the result of that, when, in this case, the Croats had to flee Vares and the Muslims came back again, again into the village. So we can consider, of course, the dramatic situation in which the population was in this context. But I repeat, a person able to save Croat, a Croat person, able to work and to hinder tension there was removed by the fundamentalist stream of the HVO and this was the result, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So here we're dealing with a region, Vitez, Busovaca in the central part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this region was, in fact, the object of such an operation. Therefore, we can agree that there were conflicts here. And I will submit a UN document; therefore, I kindly ask the usher ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence exhibit number D13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have a rather poor copy of the document, but in view of its importance and in view of the need of Professor Bianchini to comment on it, I shall read the text. We are dealing with a UN document, a letter, signed by Mr. Muhamed Sacirbey, the permanent representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations, it's dated the 21st of April, 1993, addressed to the UN Security Council, and allow me to read the text. "Recent reports of conflicts between the Bosnian and Herzegovinan army and the Croatian Defence Council have been greatly exaggerated as an ethnic conflict between Muslims and Croats. This fighting is not a conflict based along ethnic lines; rather, it is a conflict which is a consequence of the international community's armed embargo on Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the international community's failure to provide adequate humanitarian assistance to the besieged population in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina. The arms embargo denies both Muslims and Croats adequate defence capabilities in the face of barbarous aggression from Serbia and Montenegro. The armed embargo and the lack of adequate assistance pits neighbour against neighbour for control of scarce resources. If the two" -- I believe it's "parties" -- if the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: "Armies."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: "Armies," sorry. "If the two armies had adequate defence capabilities and if the population in Central Bosnia were adequately assisted with humanitarian needs, conflict between local leaders would have never occurred. Furthermore, I am pleased to report that the conflict between the two armies has subsided today as leaders from both sides have taken concrete and intensive measures to <check document> resources. Despite the conflicts over the past two days, the alliance between army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatian Defence Council will be firmly sustained. May I ask for your kind assistance in distributing this letter as a document of the Secretary-General?" Signed, Muhamed Sacirbey, Ambassador/Permanent Representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, this document has a date of the 21st of April, 1993, when, in the area of Vitez and Busovaca, the conflicts erupted. Do you agree with this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think particularly in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can remember, it's the same period when Tudjman called Izetbegovic to Zagreb and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ahmici was on the 16th of April. Would you comment on this letter, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My comment is, considering the knowledge of the whole situation, is that diplomacy had used all the arguments, all the possible arguments. This is a letter, a very amazing -- you know, this is not absolutely true, that it was the lack of the weapons that provoked the war -- the conflict between the two groups. I can understand, particularly Muslim Bosnia wanted to obtain the end of the embargo and they used all possible arguments. This is really a completely unfounded argument, because the document is -- from the document you can get the impression that the conflict started only recently while we have said that clashes, armed clashes, started for the first time, as far as I know, in mid June 1992. That is, more or less, eight months before. So I think that, you know, we have to consider that in particular the government of Bosnia had, on the one side, the need not to have a second enemy in order to resist against the Serbs and Montenegrins. Secondly, they needed in a way to stop any attempts, military attempts, or political attempts from Croatia to control one part of the territory in a way that can completely create the condition for the partition of Bosnia. So they had to move in this difficult situation in trying an alliance with Tudjman in order to resist the Serb army; at the same time, to stop Tudjman having too much influence in the area. But all the time, the aim of HVO in Croatia was linked to the idea of connecting Herceg-Bosna to Croatia, taking into consideration I have a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, excuse me for interrupting. I wish your comment of this document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's based on arguments that are not founded in truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can this be considered an official document of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? In view of the fact that it has been submitted by the permanent representative, Ambassador Sacirbey, in the United Nations to the Security Council, do you agree that in the diplomatic sense it is an official document that expresses the stance and views at that given moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a diplomatic document, official diplomatic document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Bianchini. The defence rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Niemann, do you have any questions to ask the witness in rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, in the course of your evidence, you spoke of the conflict between the HV and HVO on one side and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other side starting in April of 1993, but I take it from what you said, you're not suggesting that this was the first time that any conflict occurred between these military forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I emphasised that the first clash, according to HVO sources, according to HVO sources, was in the middle of June 1992. That is more or less when the operation to free Mostar was accomplished. I have a document, on the basis of which I am telling this, I have a document here. If you want, I can refer the exact dates, if I can look to the Court and I can refer the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document, I have the original version, Croatian version, and the translation. It's a document of the military police of Herceg-Bosna. It has been published by the administration of the military police in Lubusi in April 1995 and it is a series of reports, of articles, written by officials of the military police in order to celebrate and explain the aims of the military police in the last three years. In this document, there are very interesting things. First, it's written that the first conflicts took place with the Muslims in the middle of June 1992. Secondly, it's clarified that weapons, equipment, and help arrived to the HVO and the military police from the Croatian government since the 15th of April, 1992. It's also added that, anyway, sabotage platoons and other units, military units, existed already as Croatian sabotage platoons were in Lubusi, Mostar, and Grude, three cities of Herzegovina, since the fall of 1991. It's also explained that the training of the military police and HVO took place all in Croatia or in Herzegovina and with the help of the Croatian government. I have another document of 1993 where it's written the name of five persons sent for training to the military academy, to Zagreb, from Herceg-Bosna. I have also a very interesting document signed by Milivj Petkovic, the head, the chief of HVO, on the programme -- it's a programme of military actions -- the programme for training of the HVO, the document is of September 1992. In the document is a very interesting writing, something about instructions in patriotism, with a short programme. From this short programme it appears clear that these instructions in patriotism were focused only on the Croatian Republic and Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And another issue that arose in your discussions in cross-examination with Mr. Mikulicic related to the agreements that were entered into between the respective Presidents, Tudjman and Izetbegovic. Did any of those agreements that you know of relate to any supposed threat by Bosnian Serbs on the territory of Croatia? Did you see any agreements of that nature at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mainly, no. They include some time in some documents the problem of Croatia threatened by the Serbs but in a framework where the main focus was the situation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if there was any threat -- is it true to say that if there was any threat to Croatian territory, it was as a result of Serbs living in Croatia rather than Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a threat coming from the Serbs in Croatia who had, as an aim, to establish close ties with the Serbs in Bosnia and through them with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Finally, is it true then that the agreements that were entered into between the two Presidents were mostly related to resolution of the conflict between Bosnian Croats and -- well, I should say the HV-HVO and the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main attention was this because it was evident that none of the two, but particularly the Muslims, were unable to fight anyway against Serb and Montenegrin aggression if they had to fight against the Croats too. So they needed to solve these questions first, and this was their peculiar interest, and for this reason they tried to find a solution and a solution of all the documents we discuss today were particularly centred on the idea to find an agreement between the Muslim side and the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I should like to ask the registrar to give us document 42 and put it on the ELMO. Questions from Judge Rodrigues:

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor Bianchini, on the basis of the results of these elections, HDZ actually lost the elections. Actually, a certain agreement was reached between the Muslims and the Croats, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly, because if you speak about a lost -- loss in the elections, we have to compare with the previous election. This was the first democratic elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I wanted to, when I spoke, that they received just a little less of percentage in comparison with the influence of the Muslim community or Croatian community in the census. May I give you the comparison -- this was in comparison with the census --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Professor. Perhaps I didn't quite understand this well. The actual question is irrelevant, whether there was an agreement between the SDS and others. But you did say that other parties, when it comes to other parties, the Muslim party was led by a certain group of people, we had Zulfikarpasic and several other people. Initially they were together with Izetbegovic, if I understood you correctly, that was prior to the elections, and then later they went their separate ways. There were also some other minor parties involved. So I believe that it will be very important for you tell us something about this later parting of ways and the consequences thereof, and was the war also one of these consequences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. MBO was the party of Zulfikarpasic. Zulfikarpasic founded SDA with Izetbegovic together. Zulfikarpasic is a rich man living in Switzerland, and he lived more or less all his life abroad, outside Yugoslavia. And they were together and they had a lot of misunderstanding before the elections. So this created the condition for the split. Izetbegovic pushed particularly at that time -- insisted particularly on the aspect, Islamic aspects, while Zulfikarpasic had a more secular approach, just to give you the difference. Then after this split, Zulfikarpasic, however, had maintained good relations with Izetbegovic, and sometimes he tried to maintain even a link with Belgrade. He even suggested to establish a kind of agreement with Belgrade, and there exists a book with the minutes published by Zulfikarpasic, the title is "Okovona Bosna," It was published by him. He has an institute of research and studies in Switzerland, and they published this book after a discussion with Croatian leaders, Gotovac And others, and it explained all the attempts at creating this mediation between Karadzic, Milosevic on one side and Izetbegovic on the other side and how this attempt failed, because it failed. And then from this -- when the war erupted, Zulfikarpasic went back to Switzerland and he spent a large part of his time there but never completely outside the political situation. He put pressure on the international communities through his institute or he went, when it was possible, to Bosnia by private aeroplane. He's very rich; he has his own plane. So he had this possibility to move from one area to the another and tried to mediate and influence. This all was a stream, a circuitous stream, that any way was particularly linked to the idea to safe the integrity of Bosnia and the secular position of Bosnia while Izetbegovic was uncertain on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Another question, Professor. Could we please have document number 107? This document, Professor, has to do with the creation of the SAOs, the Serb autonomous provinces. This came under Serb control, and the Muslims and the Croats thought that the Serbs wished to take parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Muslim and the Croatian sides voted a resolution on the sovereignty of Bosnia whereas the Serb side rejected to take part in that, and this led to tensions between the two groups. These tensions escalated into aggression, and if they did, was that because -- did that lead to war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question was in these terms: This map offers you a picture of the autonomous region created by the Serbs, SDS, particularly the Serb party, between September and January -- September 1991 and January 1992, this period. The declaration of the sovereignty of Bosnia, in which the SDS did not take part, was of October. October 15, if I well remember. So this process was started but ended later. In this context, it was clear that the Serb side wanted to maintain Bosnia, whole Bosnia, or at least a large part of this Bosnia, into the Yugoslav framework federation. Yugoslavia still existed at that time. While the Croats and Muslim party, SDA, HDZ, agreed at that time to find a perspective of independence for Bosnia while they had a little bit different interpretation later. But this is another question. In this sense, the SDS didn't want to take part in the vote because it didn't want to legitimise its defeat because otherwise, you know, the numbers of the possibility to defeat the SDS, if you put together the representative of HDZ and the representative of SDA in the parliament. It refused -- this was the beginning of a process of worsening relations, because immediately after, the Serb SDS proclaimed a plebiscite in order to confirm the wish of the Serb people to remain in Yugoslavia, and they voted in November. Then you had the European Union submitting in December the proposal -- requesting to submit proposal for recognition. So in this context again, the Croats, HDZ and SDA, the Muslim party, agreed to submit, the Serbs didn't take part in the vote, and then proclaimed the republic of Serb people -- it was not Serb Republic -- republic of Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was in January. Then they ended this process. At the same time, Croatian side from November -- November 1991 and January 1992 created its own autonomous regions, the three areas. Then they made a decision, because the Badinter Commission asked for a referendum, because it was not clear the wish of the whole population because the Serbs didn't vote, asked for a referendum. The Croatian and the Serbia’s and the Muslims on side made a decision to organise the referendum. The Serb side opposed and it didn't vote. And it made the decision -- it made a decision to consider that the referendum will obligate only Croatians and Muslims but not the Serbs. You see -- you can see that everything is going on in such a way that a military clash first -- or after can happen because when you have to implement the decision of remaining in Yugoslavia or declaring independence, one of the two sides in this case will move against the other. For this reason, when the sovereignty was proclaimed, the war exploded. On the other side, you know, it's very interesting to consider the speculation, in a sense, the intellectual speculation of Bosnian General and known intellectual Sefer Halilovic, after the war, in this period, he published articles. And he suggested about the idea: Okay, we could establish an agreement with the Serbs. What might happen in this case? If you think you have the same situation, the Muslims, with an agreement with the Serbs, will create a new majority, a majority who wish to stay in Yugoslavia; and you have another party, a minority, the Croatian side, who wish not. So probably in this sense, because they already created the autonomous provinces also, you can imagine the possibility to organise some plebiscite to declare they did not agree, and so the war, in any case, was doomed to explode, from one side or the other side. This put Izetbegovic in a very difficult position in order to manage the situation between the two communities. And in this sense, his uncertainty to find his allies is another question. But this is a question connected to the whole Yugoslavia. Not one of the leaderships, policymakers of all the republics, had attempted to create a policy of alliances within Yugoslavia, including the Slovenes, but each of them sought to guarantee their own areas, and this created a situation where it was impossible to find an agreement in this sense. And that's why it was clear since the beginning of the war, in June 1991, when the war started in Slovenia, that the war will arrive -- will join Bosnia. Because -- because of this -- because the mechanism was so clear, so evident, that it was very easy to predict such an outcome, such a tragic outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Another question, Professor Bianchini. We made several references here to the HVO, the HV. I wish to know if you have specific information or opinion, do you, namely, have any information as to the relation between the HVO and the civilian authorities; for instance, by way of a small example, for someone to come to a camp, one had to have authority, permission from both the local authorities and the civilian authorities. Did you comprehend the actual relationship? Was it possible to distinguish between the civilian police, the military police, the guard, and the civilian authorities; do you have any specific opinion as to that, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. I have a document signed by -- I'm not so sure about Mate Boban, but it's a document coming from Herceg-Bosna or the command of HVO in which it is clearly stated, particularly in the case of Konjic , that all local units and police depended on the HVO. HVO was the -- temporarily military government of Herceg-Bosna. Its duty was to protect the territorial sovereignty of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian people. So in this case, HVO managed generally all the other bodies, and they were liable to it, in this sense. Even people appointed, was appointed by HVO, and HVO, the President of HVO, who was Javo Kaperlic Since 1992, was liable to the President of Herceg-Bosna, that is, directly to Mate Boban. So in this sense, it seems to me, if I can answer your question, that, yes, you have different bodies, but all these bodies, in one way or another had to answer to the HVO. And HVO had a local organisation, a structure with a local organisation and different departments. It was organised with a department, for instance, for justice, the department for -- the military department, the department for economics. Like a little government, you know? And I have also another document where it's clearly stated -- this is a document coming from the Vice-President of the Department for Justice of the HVO of September 1992, where it's clearly stated that in the area of Herceg-Bosna, the only legal system is the legal system of Herceg-Bosna. So this was a clear act in diminishing the sovereignty of the Bosnian government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Bianchini. I believe that the Chamber has no further questions, so you have just completed your testimony, and the International Criminal Tribunal thanks you for having come here and for having provided us with all this information. Before we conclude, perhaps it will be appropriate to take a look at our schedule. I believe that we continue on the 21st or the 22nd of May. We also have some other dates in our calendar which we have set. I do not seem to be able to locate it. The witness is dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I believe that you are aware of the dates which we have set in our schedule. What we need to fix is whether we shall start in the third or fourth week of August. If I have understood you properly, Mr. Niemann will not be here in the third week of August. Is that so, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I won't be here for the first week of August, but after that, I'm here continuously. So it's just the first week of August that is a difficulty for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay, the first week. Thank you. So we will work things out. It is a bit difficult for the second week of August. Probably, most probably, the third and the fourth weeks will be convenient for both parties and we will continue our work in one of those weeks. That will be all for today. I wish you a pleasant weekend. To you, the interpreters in the technical booth, I thank you all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just so it makes things easier for everyone to know where they are, that is the evidence of the Prosecution, and I close the Prosecution case on the completion of Professor Bianchini's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I believe that we had all gathered that. And it is up to you, Mr. Mikulicic, the next time we convene, to present us with your opening statement and to introduce your witnesses. Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: at 1.20 p.m.
